Refused.description:
The command was not carried out. The body holds the refusal under `error`, with its code; a caller reads the code, and the status is worked out from it:

| Status | Codes |
|---|---|
| 400 | `bad_json` |
| 401 | `unauthenticated` |
| 403 | `forbidden`, `reason_required` |
| 404 | `unknown_class`, `unknown_document`, `unknown_table`, `unknown_schema`, `unknown_blob`, `unknown_action`, `unknown_row`, `unknown_user`, `unknown_inlet`, `unknown_key`, `unknown_command` |
| 409 | `key_reused`, `duplicate`, `terminal`, `wrong_state`, `guard_false` |
| 413 | `blob_too_large`, `too_large` |
| 499 | `caller_left` |
| 500 | `storage`, `internal` |
| 503 | `closed`, `busy` |
| 504 | `timeout` |
| 422 | every other refusal |

info.description:
Every call that reads or changes a database is a command: a name and one JSON object, answered by one JSON object. A command is sent as `POST /v1/<command>` with its object as the body. A command that reads is a `POST` too, and the id of a document travels in the JSON and never in the address.

Who sends a request is never in the command. A database that keeps its own users is sent a key of a user, as `Authorization: Bearer fado_…`. A member that is `null` is a member left out, and a member a command does not have is refused.

This document is written from the engine's own table of the commands. The manual's chapter on the commands is written from the same table.

post.description: The message is in its sender's own form and carries no key of a user: it proves who sent it as the inlet says, with a secret shown or a signature in a header. The database carries out the one command the message becomes, as the user the inlet names, and a message sent twice makes one commit. The answer says what happened and nothing of the database: a refusal holds a code and no words. Only a door that was told to take messages does; `fadodb serve` is told by the member `inbound` of its settings.

200.description: The stream is open. The reply does not end: it carries one entry for each event the caller may read of, in the form of server-sent events. An entry is three lines and an empty one: `id:` with the id of the event, `event: change`, and `data:` with the event as one JSON object on one line. A line that begins with a colon is a comment. When the server ends the stream, the last entry is `event: end`, whose data is a refusal.
